title: My Sock Is Still Wet From Asia's Rainiest Village
question: Why do people live in Mawsynram?
message: This video tells curious adults that people live in Mawsynram because the monsoon rain that soaks its hilltop runs down to water farmed slopes of areca nut, betel leaf, pepper and broom grass, making it the centre of a block of about 160 villages, and because by Khasi custom a family house is kept in trust rather than sold, even though the same fast-running water leaves these hills short of drinking water in the dry season.
angle: People live in Mawsynram because the monsoon that drenches its hilltop runs straight down to water the slopes below, where families grow areca nut, betel leaf, black pepper, jackfruit, broom grass and bamboo and make brooms and baskets at home, which makes the village the centre of a development block of about 160 villages with a health centre and a road down toward Bangladesh, and because by Khasi custom the family house is kept by the youngest daughter for the whole lineage rather than sold; despite rain that would stand almost twelve metres deep in a year, falls mostly in four months and, around these hills, mostly at night, clouds that drift indoors, landslides that sometimes cut villages off, and a dry season when that same fast-running water leaves some villages short of drinking water.

scenes.narration: The village is Mawsynram, in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, on the edge of a plateau above Bangladesh. I went there in June to move in, with every sock I own. I came home with this one, a small broom, and a bottle of water I paid for. In one of the rainiest places on Earth, I paid for water. By the end of this trip, the broom and the bottle explained more than the rain did. But first, I had some very confident wrong ideas.

scenes.narration: I arrived in a taxi with its wipers on full panic. My first theory was fame. A place this wet must live off being wet. The World Meteorological Organization lists Mawsynram as the record holder for average yearly rainfall in Asia. About eleven thousand eight hundred and seventy-two millimetres, averaged from nineteen forty-one to nineteen seventy-nine. That's about four hundred and sixty-seven inches. Left to pile up, one year of it would stand almost twelve metres deep. About thirty-nine feet. Taller than a three-storey house. Is it the wettest place on the whole planet? Depending on who's measuring. Nearby Cherrapunji and two spots in Colombia have numbers of their own. So I went looking for the fame. A rain museum is on the way. It isn't open yet. Nobody moves house for a museum that isn't open yet. My second theory was that the rain keeps everyone in. So I asked a taxi to take me out. It did. Shillong is about sixty kilometres away by road, under forty miles. Landslides block roads around here sometimes, and in the wettest months the rain can cut some villages off for weeks. But the road works, both ways. I rode out, had a dry cup of tea, and rode back. Nobody was trapped. They could leave. They stay.

scenes.narration: On my second morning I went out with an umbrella. A good one. The rain came in sideways. The umbrella turned inside out, then outside in, then left without me. That's when I met the knup. It's a rain shield, woven from bamboo and layered with dried palm leaves, sometimes with a plastic sheet these days. It sits over your head and back and reaches down to your knees. Basically, a roof you wear. Women here make them. I got one, put it on, and stood in a downpour, dry, hands in my pockets, like a very smug tortoise. Then I saw what the free hands are for. People in knups were heading down the slopes below the village. The slopes are farms. Areca nut. Betel leaf. Black pepper. Jackfruit. Broom grass. Bamboo. This is the part I had backwards. The rain that soaks the hilltop runs downhill and waters all of it. What drowns my socks up here feeds the farms down there.

scenes.narration: Then the broom made sense. Families here turn broom grass into brooms and bamboo into baskets, right at home. Broom grass is one of the area's main cash crops. I tried to make a broom. It came out shaped like a question mark. And Mawsynram is more than one village. In the twenty eleven census, it was the centre of a development block of well over a hundred villages, with around fifty-four thousand people. Its health centre sends a team out to nearby villages every month. One of their drivers has said these slopes wear out his brake pads about every two weeks. A road runs from these hills down toward the border with Bangladesh. So the hilltop is where things meet. Crops on the slopes below. Roads and markets beyond. People here don't live in the rain because they love rain. They live where the rain pays off. I hung the broom on my backpack and unpacked one sock. Just one.

scenes.narration: That still left the question my socks kept asking. Why does it rain this much here? I assumed the sea must be right next door. It isn't. The Bay of Bengal is far to the south, beyond the flat plains of Bangladesh. That flatness is the trick. In the monsoon, warm wet air blows north off the bay, and across the plain nothing gets in its way. Then it hits this plateau. Mawsynram sits about fourteen hundred metres up, roughly forty-seven hundred feet. The air is shoved up the slope. It cools, and its water falls out. It works like the lid on a pot of soup. Steam rises, meets the cool lid, and drips back down. These hills are the lid. I was standing on it, in June, in a raincoat.

scenes.narration: The rain also keeps odd hours. According to satellite studies of these hills, the heaviest rain tends to come between midnight and early morning. I hung my laundry out on a bright afternoon. By breakfast it was wetter than when I washed it. When AFP visited in twenty thirteen, its reporter wrote that clouds sometimes drift right into homes and leave everything damp. One drifted into my room and settled on my bed. I slept on the floor. A Khasi poet has written about the local words for different rains. One of them, lapiwtung, is a rain that makes your clothes smell. There are words for a rain that lasts six nights, and one that lasts nine. My suitcase met lapiwtung. That night, the sock I had unpacked went back in. The same report said that when the rains finally end, there is no festival. People just carry their clothes outside to dry.

scenes.narration: So I went back in January and did exactly that. I carried my sock outside. It dried in an afternoon. I nearly framed it. I unpacked the whole suitcase. I couldn't find official monthly averages for Mawsynram, so I borrowed the ones from nearby Cherrapunji. There, about three quarters of the year's rain falls between June and September. An average July day brings more rain than the whole of December. The dry season really is dry. And here's where my bottle of water comes in. In twenty twenty-four, the local member of the state assembly said some villages here run short of drinking water in the dry months. The water doesn't stay up on the hilltops, and streams can run dry. A headmistress told a reporter in twenty twenty that people never learned to save water, because there was always so much of it. The same report described rainwater tanks built by the government and villagers together, one for each neighbourhood. The headman said that because people built them, they treat them as their own. I stood beside an empty stream bed, in one of the rainiest corners of Asia, drinking water I had bought.

scenes.narration: On a clear dry day, from the edge of the plateau, you can see the plains of Bangladesh. I tried to follow one June raindrop in my head. It lands on my sock. It rolls off, joins a stream, races down the slope, and drops over the edge. Lovely form. The hilltop is a steep tin roof. Pour a bucket on it, and it gets very wet, very fast, and keeps almost nothing. In twenty nineteen, Meghalaya's deputy chief minister said much the same: the state's rain runs off quickly, into Bangladesh. Sometimes the run-off is enormous. On the seventeenth of June, twenty twenty-two, Mawsynram recorded more than a metre of rain in twenty-four hours. That's over thirty-nine inches. Bangladesh's flood forecasters named heavy rain in Meghalaya and Assam as one cause of the floods that followed in the Sylhet region. Millions of people were affected. The hill catches the rain. The plain catches what the hill can't hold.

scenes.narration: Before flying home, I opened my notebook map and drew one more dotted line, south and east, down to Khasi and Jaintia villages on the lower slopes. That's where most of the living root bridges grow. Villagers guide the hanging roots of a rubber fig tree across a stream, until they reach the far bank and take hold. Then they wait. The people who start a bridge are not always the ones who finish it. Estimates vary for how long a bridge takes, from about twenty years to several decades. Some bridges are still growing stronger after more than sixty years. India nominated them for World Heritage status in January twenty twenty-six, and UNESCO is due to look at them in twenty twenty-seven. I crossed one very slowly, stepping only where the roots looked confident. Nobody plants a bridge in a place they mean to leave.

By custom, the youngest daughter, called ka khadduh, keeps the ancestral house and the family land. Keeps, not owns. It belongs to the whole lineage, and selling it needs the agreement of her mother's brothers and her own brothers. That custom is being debated right now. But you can see what it does. It's a bit like a family's one spare key, held by the person everyone trusts. A house like that isn't something you sell because the weather got on your nerves.

The rain that soaks the hilltop runs down to feed the slopes, and the families up top keep houses that were kept for them. I just couldn't keep my things dry. A cloud took my bed. verdict.reason: People in Mawsynram live where the monsoon pays off: the rain that soaks the hilltop runs down to water farmed slopes of areca nut, betel leaf, pepper and broom grass, the village is the centre of about 160 villages, and by Khasi custom family houses are kept in trust; but a cloud in Wob's bed, rain that comes mostly at night, lapiwtung in the suitcase and a sock still damp since June mean Wob could not keep anything dry. claims.quote: The village that did this sits in the hills of northeast India.
claims.statement: Mawsynram, a village (in fact a cluster of villages) in the Khasi Hills of the state of Meghalaya, lies in the hills of northeast India.

claims.quote: The village is Mawsynram, in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, on the edge of a plateau above Bangladesh.
claims.statement: Mawsynram is in the East Khasi Hills district of Meghalaya, India, at about 1,431 m on the southern edge of the Meghalaya (Khasi) plateau, above the low plains of Bangladesh's Sylhet region.

claims.quote: In one of the rainiest places on Earth, I paid for water.
claims.statement: Mawsynram is one of the rainiest places on Earth: the World Meteorological Organization lists it as having the greatest average annual rainfall in its Asia region (11,872 mm, 1941–1979).

claims.quote: The World Meteorological Organization lists Mawsynram as the record holder for average yearly rainfall in Asia. About eleven thousand eight hundred and seventy-two millimetres, averaged from nineteen forty-one to nineteen seventy-nine. That's about four hundred and sixty-seven inches.
claims.statement: The World Meteorological Organization lists Mawsynram, India, as the record for the greatest average annual rainfall in WMO Region II (Asia): 11,872 mm (467.4 inches), based on data from 1941 to 1979 (38 years of record).

claims.quote: Left to pile up, one year of it would stand almost twelve metres deep. About thirty-nine feet. Taller than a three-storey house.
claims.statement: An average annual rainfall of 11,872 mm corresponds to a water depth of about 11.9 metres (about 39 feet), more than the height of a typical three-storey house (roughly 9–10 metres).

claims.quote: Is it the wettest place on the whole planet? Depending on who's measuring. Nearby Cherrapunji and two spots in Colombia have numbers of their own.
claims.statement: Whether Mawsynram is the wettest place on Earth is disputed: nearby Cherrapunji (Sohra) holds the WMO world record for the greatest 12-month rainfall (26,470 mm, August 1860 to July 1861) and has a comparable long-term average; Lloró and López de Micay in Colombia have reported higher average annual rainfall that the WMO has not evaluated; and in 2013 an India Meteorological Department official said it could not be concluded with certainty which place is wettest.

claims.quote: A rain museum is on the way. It isn't open yet.
claims.statement: The Meghalaya government has a rain museum project at Mawsynram (proposed in December 2025); the museum was not yet open as of late 2026.

claims.quote: Shillong is about sixty kilometres away by road, under forty miles.
claims.statement: Mawsynram is about 60 km (under 40 miles) by road from Shillong; Meghalaya Tourism gives the distance as 61 km.

claims.quote: Landslides block roads around here sometimes, and in the wettest months the rain can cut some villages off for weeks.
claims.statement: Landslides sometimes block roads in the Mawsynram block (for example at km 33 of the Mawphlang–Balat road on 4 April 2022), and during the rainy months (about May to October) heavy rain can cut off some villages in the Mawsynram area for weeks.

claims.quote: It's a rain shield, woven from bamboo and layered with dried palm leaves, sometimes with a plastic sheet these days. It sits over your head and back and reaches down to your knees.
claims.statement: The knup is a traditional Khasi rain shield used around Mawsynram and Cherrapunji: a woven bamboo frame waterproofed with dried palm leaves (sometimes plastic sheeting today), worn over the head and back and reaching down to about the knees.

claims.quote: Women here make them.
claims.statement: Knups in Meghalaya are made by women, using bamboo moulds and broad-bladed knives; AFP reported in 2013 that women in Mawsynram weave knups during the rainy season.

claims.quote: Then I saw what the free hands are for. People in knups were heading down the slopes below the village.
claims.statement: Because the knup is worn on the head and back rather than held, it leaves both hands free, which lets wearers work on steep hillside fields in the rain.

claims.quote: The slopes are farms. Areca nut. Betel leaf. Black pepper. Jackfruit. Broom grass. Bamboo.
claims.statement: Villages in the Mawsynram area (for example Kenmynsaw, in Mawsynram subdivision) grow areca nut, betel leaf, black pepper, jackfruit, broom grass and bamboo on the hill slopes.

claims.quote: The rain that soaks the hilltop runs downhill and waters all of it.
claims.statement: The heavy monsoon rain that falls on the hilltops around Mawsynram does not stay there but runs off quickly down the steep slopes, the same slopes where crops such as areca nut, betel leaf, pepper and broom grass are grown.

claims.quote: Families here turn broom grass into brooms and bamboo into baskets, right at home. Broom grass is one of the area's main cash crops.
claims.statement: Families in villages of the Mawsynram area make brooms and baskets at home from broom grass and bamboo, and broom grass is one of the area's main crops for sale.

claims.quote: In the twenty eleven census, it was the centre of a development block of well over a hundred villages, with around fifty-four thousand people.
claims.statement: Mawsynram is the headquarters of the Mawsynram community development (C&RD) block in East Khasi Hills, Meghalaya, which had 54,109 people living in well over a hundred villages in the 2011 Census of India.

claims.quote: Its health centre sends a team out to nearby villages every month. One of their drivers has said these slopes wear out his brake pads about every two weeks.
claims.statement: The Community Health Centre at Mawsynram runs monthly mobile health outreach clinics to nearby villages; a taxi driver who carries the health team told WHO India (2024) that he has to change his brake pads about every two weeks because of the steep roads.

claims.quote: A road runs from these hills down toward the border with Bangladesh.
claims.statement: The Mawphlang–Balat road runs through the Mawsynram block, from the Khasi Hills down toward the India–Bangladesh border at Balat.

claims.quote: I assumed the sea must be right next door. It isn't. The Bay of Bengal is far to the south, beyond the flat plains of Bangladesh.
claims.statement: Mawsynram is not on the coast: the Bay of Bengal lies far to the south of the Meghalaya plateau, beyond the low, flat plains of Bangladesh.

claims.quote: In the monsoon, warm wet air blows north off the bay, and across the plain nothing gets in its way. Then it hits this plateau. Mawsynram sits about fourteen hundred metres up, roughly forty-seven hundred feet. The air is shoved up the slope. It cools, and its water falls out.
claims.statement: During the summer monsoon, warm moist air from the Bay of Bengal flows north across the flat Bangladesh plains and is forced up the steep southern slopes of the Meghalaya plateau (Mawsynram lies at about 1,431 m, roughly 4,700 feet), where it cools and its moisture condenses into very heavy orographic rainfall.

claims.quote: According to satellite studies of these hills, the heaviest rain tends to come between midnight and early morning.
claims.statement: Satellite-based studies (Ohsawa et al. 2001; Romatschke and Houze 2011, cited by Sato 2013) found that rainfall around the Meghalaya plateau peaks from around midnight to early morning, associated with a nocturnal low-level wind from the Bangladesh plains striking the southern slopes; hourly records at Cherrapunji (1946–1949) also showed more rain from 1 to 7 a.m. No hourly rainfall data exist for Mawsynram itself.

claims.quote: When AFP visited in twenty thirteen, its reporter wrote that clouds sometimes drift right into homes and leave everything damp.
claims.statement: A 2013 AFP report from Mawsynram described clouds sometimes drifting into homes and leaving a damp film on belongings.

claims.quote: A Khasi poet has written about the local words for different rains. One of them, lapiwtung, is a rain that makes your clothes smell. There are words for a rain that lasts six nights, and one that lasts nine.
claims.statement: Khasi poet Kynpham Sing Nongkynrih has written that the Khasi language has many words for different kinds of rain, including lapiwtung, a rain that makes clothes smell, lap-hynriew-miet, a rain lasting six nights, and lap-khyndai-miet, a rain lasting nine nights.

claims.quote: The same report said that when the rains finally end, there is no festival. People just carry their clothes outside to dry.
claims.statement: According to the 2013 AFP report, Mawsynram's village headman said that when the monsoon rains end there is no celebration; people simply bring their clothes outside to dry.

claims.quote: I couldn't find official monthly averages for Mawsynram, so I borrowed the ones from nearby Cherrapunji. There, about three quarters of the year's rain falls between June and September. An average July day brings more rain than the whole of December. The dry season really is dry.
claims.statement: At nearby Cherrapunji, Japan Meteorological Agency monthly normals show about 75% of annual rainfall falling from June to September, and an average July day (about 95 mm) brings more rain than the whole of December (about 8 mm).

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-four, the local member of the state assembly said some villages here run short of drinking water in the dry months. The water doesn't stay up on the hilltops, and streams can run dry.
claims.statement: In January 2024, Mawsynram's member of the Meghalaya Legislative Assembly, Olan Singh Suin, said some villages in the area run short of drinking water in the dry season because water does not stay on the high hills, and that streams sometimes dry up.

claims.quote: A headmistress told a reporter in twenty twenty that people never learned to save water, because there was always so much of it.
claims.statement: In a January 2020 AFP report from Mawsynram, headmistress Miralin Kharchandy said residents had never learned to save water because there was water all around them.

claims.quote: The same report described rainwater tanks built by the government and villagers together, one for each neighbourhood. The headman said that because people built them, they treat them as their own.
claims.statement: The same 2020 AFP report described rainwater-harvesting tanks built in Mawsynram by the authorities together with residents for each locality; village headman Tarcisius Dhkar said residents built them themselves and so regard the tanks as their own.

claims.quote: I stood beside an empty stream bed, in one of the rainiest corners of Asia, drinking water I had bought.
claims.statement: Mawsynram, which the WMO lists as having Asia's greatest average annual rainfall, nonetheless faces dry-season water shortages, with springs, streams and lakes in the area drying up.

claims.quote: On a clear dry day, from the edge of the plateau, you can see the plains of Bangladesh.
claims.statement: From the southern edge of the Meghalaya plateau around Mawsynram, the plains of Bangladesh are visible on clear days in the dry season.

claims.quote: The hilltop is a steep tin roof. Pour a bucket on it, and it gets very wet, very fast, and keeps almost nothing.
claims.statement: On the steep, rocky hills around Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, monsoon rain runs off quickly rather than soaking in, so very little of it is retained on the hilltops.

claims.quote: In twenty nineteen, Meghalaya's deputy chief minister said much the same: the state's rain runs off quickly, into Bangladesh.
claims.statement: In July 2019, when Meghalaya's cabinet approved a draft water policy, Deputy Chief Minister Prestone Tynsong said the state's rainwater is not retained and flows quickly into Bangladesh because of the steep terrain.

claims.quote: On the seventeenth of June, twenty twenty-two, Mawsynram recorded more than a metre of rain in twenty-four hours. That's over thirty-nine inches.
claims.statement: The India Meteorological Department recorded 1,003.6 mm (about 39.5 inches) of rain at Mawsynram in the 24 hours to 17 June 2022.

claims.quote: Bangladesh's flood forecasters named heavy rain in Meghalaya and Assam as one cause of the floods that followed in the Sylhet region. Millions of people were affected.
claims.statement: In June 2022, Bangladesh's Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre cited extremely heavy rainfall in Meghalaya and Assam as one cause of the floods in Bangladesh's Sylhet region, which affected millions of people.

claims.quote: drew one more dotted line, south and east, down to Khasi and Jaintia villages on the lower slopes. That's where most of the living root bridges grow.
claims.statement: Living root bridges are found in Khasi and Jaintia villages in the hills of Meghalaya, mostly on the lower slopes (a 2015–2017 survey found most between about 250 and 900 m).

claims.quote: Villagers guide the hanging roots of a rubber fig tree across a stream, until they reach the far bank and take hold.
claims.statement: Living root bridges are made by guiding the aerial roots of the rubber fig tree (Ficus elastica) across a stream, often along bamboo or other supports, until they root on the far bank.

claims.quote: The people who start a bridge are not always the ones who finish it. Estimates vary for how long a bridge takes, from about twenty years to several decades. Some bridges are still growing stronger after more than sixty years.
claims.statement: Living root bridges can take longer than a single generation to build: estimates of how long one takes to become usable vary, with UNDP giving 20 to 25 years and Ludwig et al. (2019) describing a process over generations, decades to centuries, including a bridge still not at full function after 66 years; the bridges keep growing and strengthening over time.

claims.quote: India nominated them for World Heritage status in January twenty twenty-six, and UNESCO is due to look at them in twenty twenty-seven.
claims.statement: In January 2026 India submitted Meghalaya's living root bridges ('Jingkieng Jri / Lyucharai Cultural Landscape') to UNESCO for World Heritage status, for examination by the World Heritage Committee in 2027.

claims.quote: Khasi families trace their line through the mother. By custom, the youngest daughter, called ka khadduh, keeps the ancestral house and the family land. Keeps, not owns. It belongs to the whole lineage, and selling it needs the agreement of her mother's brothers and her own brothers.
claims.statement: The Khasi are matrilineal: descent is traced through the mother, and by custom the youngest daughter (ka khadduh) is the custodian, not the individual owner, of the ancestral house and family property, which belong to the lineage; selling it traditionally requires the consent of her maternal uncles and brothers.

claims.quote: That custom is being debated right now.
claims.statement: The Khasi inheritance custom is under debate: a Khasi Inheritance of Property Bill proposed in 2021 (equal division of property among children) remains pending at the Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council, which revived its review in June 2026.
